We’ll also cover the crucial difference between visible emission and emission that contributes to indirect lighting, and the practical steps to mark an object static and include its emission in baked Global Illumination. A glowing rune can be purely decorative, or it can actually tint nearby surfaces when baked correctly — the difference affects realism and performance. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to set up a glowing rune stone, choose the right GI mode, and avoid common pitfalls like over-bright emission or unnecessary real-time GI costs. Think of this as the toolset you use when light needs to both look right and behave affordably.

screens.title: Directional, Point, and Spot Lights
screens.narratorSegment: Start by identifying what each Unity light type is meant to simulate and why that matters for materials. Directional lights act like the sun: they send parallel rays across the scene and create consistent full-scene illumination and long, crisp shadows. Use them where you need a dominant, uniform light source. Point lights emit from a single point in all directions and are ideal for bulbs or embers; they produce radial falloff so highlights are localized and bright near the source but dim quickly with distance. Spot lights are a constrained point light that emits inside a cone, useful for flashlights or stage lights that need both directionality and a falloff profile. Concretely, on a PBR sphere a highly metallic, smooth surface will show a hard, small highlight from a point light and a softer elongated highlight from a directional source. A rough surface diffuses those highlights into broad soft patches. A common misconception is to treat all lights as interchangeable: the visual cues and shadow behavior are different and affect perceived material type. To practice, place a neutral PBR sphere, toggle lights on and off, and observe how the same material reads metallic under one light and matte under another. Which light makes the material read as polished or worn? That observation will guide your placement decisions in a scene and help you balance realism with performance.

keyIdea.title: Light types matter
keyIdea.text: Directional = uniform sun-like lighting, Point = radial local emitter, Spot = cone-shaped directional emitter; each produces distinct highlights and falloff on PBR materials.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Light Types Comparison
Light type behaviors
Compare how each light affects highlights, falloff, and shadows on PBR materials.
Directional
Parallel rays, consistent shadows, good for sun/moon. Produces broad highlights on roughness contrasts.
Point
Omnidirectional falloff, bright near source, sharp speculars on smooth metals.
Spot
Cone-shaped, useful for focused illumination with directional falloff and penumbra control.
Concrete example and practice
A smooth metallic sphere shows a crisp bright dot under a Point light, while a rough non-metallic sphere reads as soft under the same light. Use this difference to sell material type.
Practice
  • Place a neutral PBR sphere and add a Point light. Observe highlight size and intensity.
  • Increase smoothness and note the highlight narrowing and brightening.
  • Swap to a Directional light and compare shadow direction and global contrast.
Common misconception
Not all lights are interchangeable: using a directional light to mimic a nearby lamp will flatten falloff and break believable proximity cues.
Key Takeaway

Match light type to physical source: choose Directional for sun, Point for bulbs/embers, and Spot for cones; combine them with material properties to craft believable highlights and shadows.

screens.title: PBR Material Properties and Light
screens.narratorSegment: To predict how a material will look under lighting, you need a clear definition of the core PBR channels. Albedo defines the base color that diffusely reflects light. It controls the hue and visible surface pigmentation that remains under diffuse illumination. Metallic is a boolean-like range that decides whether reflections carry the surface tint (metallic) or remain neutral (dielectric). A metallic surface reflects environment colors strongly and darkens its diffuse contribution, while a non-metal retains its albedo as the diffuse result. Smoothness controls microfacet distribution: higher smoothness yields narrow, high-intensity specular highlights that mirror the light source, while low smoothness scatters reflection energy into broad, soft highlights. Concretely, a bright point light on a smooth metal creates a crisp pinprick highlight; on a rough non-metal it becomes a soft, spread highlight. A common mistake is to push smoothness and metallic values to extremes without considering environment reflections and exposure controls — this can yield blown-out highlights or a plastic look. Practice adjusting each channel on the same geometry while keeping lighting constant: you’ll see how simple numeric changes dramatically alter material read and perceived realism.

keyIdea.title: PBR channels
keyIdea.text: Albedo sets base color; Metallic controls whether reflections carry color; Smoothness sets highlight size and clarity — together they define surface response to light.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › PBR Material Channels
Core channels and meanings
Understand what each channel does so you can predict real lighting responses.
Albedo
Base color that controls diffuse reflection and visible pigmentation under neutral lighting.
Metallic
When high, reflections carry surface tint and diffuse energy is reduced; when low, reflections remain neutral.
Smoothness
Controls microfacet sharpness: high for mirror-like highlights, low for matte, diffused scattering.
Concrete example
Take a stone material: Albedo dark gray, Metallic near 0, Smoothness low. Under a warm Point light you get soft, warm illumination and subtle fuzzed highlights.
Practice
Set a sphere: vary smoothness from 0.1 to 0.9 and watch highlights narrow and intensify. Toggle metallic to see color in reflections.
Misconception
High smoothness is not always better. Excessive smoothness without environment detail looks like overpolished plastic.
Key Takeaway

Adjust Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness together while keeping lighting constant to predict the final appearance of a material under scene lights.

screens.title: What is an Emission Map?
screens.narratorSegment: An Emission map is a texture that tells the shader which parts of a surface should appear lit regardless of scene lighting. White areas in the emission texture produce full emission, black areas have none, and gray values yield partial emission. You can pair that map with an Emission Color and an Intensity multiplier to control hue and perceived brightness. Artistically, emission is perfect for screens, neon, glowing veins, or magical runes. Technically, emission overrides the normal lighting calculation for those pixels and makes them render as if they are bright. A key practical note: by default emission only affects the object's own shading; it makes pixels look bright but does not necessarily light other objects. To make emission contribute to scene lighting you must enable its Global Illumination contribution and select a baked or realtime mode depending on your needs. A common error is using very high emission intensity without adjusting exposure and post-processing, which can blow out details and hide texture contrast. When authoring emission maps, keep the pattern clear, preview the result in different exposure settings, and test both with and without additional explicit light sources for directional cues.

keyIdea.title: Emission map basics
keyIdea.text: Emission maps mark glow regions; Emission Color and Intensity shape hue and perceived brightness; enable GI to let emission light the environment.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Emission Map
How emission maps work
A grayscale texture controls per-pixel emission; pair it with color and intensity for artistic control.
Map rules
White = full emission, black = none, gray = partial. Use masks to isolate glow areas like screens or runes.
Color & intensity
Choose an emission color and an intensity multiplier to match scene exposure and artistic intent.
Example: sci-fi panel
Use an albedo for base detail and a separate UV-aligned emission map for buttons and indicators. Set emission to vibrant blue and tune intensity for readability in-game.
Practice
Create a simple black-and-white rune texture. Assign it to the Emission slot and adjust intensity while viewing in scene exposure.
Misconception
Emission alone does not necessarily illuminate other objects unless GI contribution is enabled and baked or realtime GI is used.
Key Takeaway

Emission maps let pixels look self-lit; use color and intensity carefully and enable GI contribution when you want surrounding surfaces to receive light from that glow.

screens.title: Emission: Visual vs. Scene Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: A recurring source of confusion is the difference between emission as a visual effect and emission as a contributor to scene lighting. By default, enabling Emission on a material makes pixels render as if they are bright, but that brightness is local to the object’s shader; it affects how the object looks to the camera, not necessarily how it lights neighboring geometry. To make emission influence the rest of the scene, you must enable Global Illumination on the material and pick either Baked or Realtime in the Emission GI dropdown. Baked GI records emission into lightmaps for static geometry, allowing glowing objects to tint nearby surfaces affordably. Realtime GI, if available and enabled, allows dynamic objects to contribute to indirect lighting but at a higher runtime cost. An example: a glowing rune on a static stone with Emission GI set to Baked will create a subtle colored bleed onto surrounding walls after baking. A common mistake is assuming emission replaces actual lights; emission adds ambient tint but does not cast precise shadows or directional illumination. When you need directional cues and crisp shadows, combine emission with a low-intensity Point or Spot light for the right mix of atmosphere and readable lighting.

keyIdea.title: Visual vs lighting
keyIdea.text: Emission can be purely visual or, when configured for GI, baked or realtime to affect indirect lighting; combine with real lights for direction and shadows.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Emission: Visual vs Scene Light
Visual emission
Makes pixels appear bright on the object itself but doesn't automatically light the environment.
What you see
The object looks glowing even in dark scenes because the shader outputs brightness for those pixels.
When environment is affected
Set Emission GI to Baked or Realtime and bake lighting, or use Realtime GI, to allow emission to contribute indirect lighting.
Concrete example
A rune stone with Emission only looks bright; set Emission GI to Baked and mark static, then bake to make the surrounding plane pick up a subtle colored tint.
Practice steps
Enable emission, set GI to Baked, mark object Static, open Lighting settings and Generate Lighting. Observe lightmap tint changes.
Pitfall
Relying only on emission for directional lighting removes cues and realistic shadows; combine with low-intensity real lights for clarity.
Key Takeaway

Enable Emission GI and bake for static glow that affects surroundings; use realtime GI only when dynamic contribution is strictly required and budget allows.

screens.title: Global Illumination: Baked vs Realtime
screens.narratorSegment: Global Illumination simulates how light bounces and contributes to the indirect illumination in a scene. There are two practical approaches you will use in Unity: baked lighting and realtime lighting. Baked lighting precomputes indirect lighting into lightmaps for static geometry; this is extremely efficient at runtime and produces stable, high-quality indirect lighting for environments that do not change. Realtime lighting updates every frame and allows dynamic objects and lights to affect indirect illumination, but it costs more C P U or G P U time and can be harder to optimize. For emission, baked GI is the most common approach: set Emission GI to Baked, mark the glowing object as static, and generate lighting so the emission is stored into the lightmap and tints neighboring surfaces. Realtime GI should be reserved for cases where glowing elements move or change intensity at runtime and your target platform can afford the cost. A common confusion is thinking baked lightmaps are low-quality; when tuned with proper resolution and bake settings, they provide natural-looking indirect color bleeding without the runtime expense. Choose the method that balances visual fidelity and platform performance for your project.

narration.text: Global Illumination simulates how light bounces and contributes to the indirect illumination in a scene. There are two practical approaches you will use in Unity: baked lighting and realtime lighting. Baked lighting precomputes indirect lighting into lightmaps for static geometry; this is extremely efficient at runtime and produces stable, high-quality indirect lighting for environments that do not change. Realtime lighting updates every frame and allows dynamic objects and lights to affect indirect illumination, but it costs more C P U or G P U time and can be harder to optimize. Realtime GI should be reserved for cases where glowing elements move or change intensity at runtime and your target platform can afford the cost. A common confusion is thinking baked lightmaps are low-quality; when tuned with proper resolution and bake settings, they provide natural-looking indirect color bleeding without the runtime expense. Choose the method that balances visual fidelity and platform performance for your project.

keyIdea.title: GI tradeoffs
keyIdea.text: Baked GI is performant and stable for static scenes; Realtime GI supports dynamic changes but has higher runtime cost and complexity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Global Illumination
Baked GI
Precomputes indirect lighting into textures for static geometry. Efficient at runtime and great for stable environments.
When to use
Static scenes or static parts of a scene where you want affordable high-quality indirect light and color bleeding.
How emission fits
Set material Emission GI to Baked and mark object Static so its glow is baked into lightmaps as indirect light.
Realtime GI
Updates indirect lighting each frame and supports dynamic elements but at higher runtime cost and complexity.
When to use
Use for moving emissive objects or when light intensity changes during gameplay and budget allows.
Tradeoffs
Realtime GI can be expensive; profile and prefer baked GI for static scene elements to save memory and CPU/GPU time.
Key Takeaway

Prefer baked GI for static emission to get cheap indirect lighting; reserve realtime GI for dynamic needs and always consider performance tradeoffs.

screens.title: Configure Materials to Contribute to GI
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a material and its objects to contribute emission to Global Illumination is a straightforward inspector workflow, but missing a step will prevent emission from affecting the scene. Begin by selecting your material in the Project window. In the material Inspector find the Emission section, check the Emission checkbox, and assign your Emission map and color. Important: set the Emission 'Global Illumination' dropdown to the desired mode — choose Baked for static contribution or Realtime for dynamic contribution if your project supports it. Next, select the object using that material in the Hierarchy and set its 'Static' checkbox in the top-right of the Inspector so Unity considers it for lightmapping. Open Window → Rendering → Lighting → Settings and ensure 'Auto Generate' is off if you want manual control. Then click 'Generate Lighting' to bake. After baking, inspect lightmaps to confirm the tint from emission appears on surrounding static geometry. A common oversight is forgetting to mark the object static or leaving Emission GI on 'None'; either omission will stop indirect illumination from being saved. Always re-bake after making changes to emission color or intensity, because lightmaps are generated from the current emission settings at bake time.

keyIdea.title: Bake workflow
keyIdea.text: Set Emission GI to Baked, mark object Static, and Generate Lighting to capture emission into lightmaps.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Material → GI Configuration
Inspector steps
A clear checklist prevents missed steps when baking emission into lightmaps.
1. Enable Emission
Check Emission, assign Emission Map, choose Emission Color and set Intensity.
2. Set GI mode
In Emission dropdown select 'Baked' for static contribution or 'Realtime' if needed and supported.
3. Mark object Static
Select the object in Hierarchy and enable the Static checkbox so it is included in lightmapping.
Baking steps
Control baking from the Lighting window to produce lightmaps that include emission contribution.
Open Lighting Settings
Window → Rendering → Lighting → Settings. Uncheck Auto Generate for manual control if preferred.
Generate Lighting
Click Generate Lighting to bake; inspect the lightmaps and scene to confirm the emission tint.
Common oversight
Forgetting to mark the object Static or leaving Emission GI on 'None' are the most frequent reasons emission does not affect the bake.
Key Takeaway

Follow the Inspector checklist and bake process: enable emission, choose GI mode, mark static, then generate lighting to capture emission into lightmaps.

screens.title: Activity: Create a Glowing Rune Stone (Step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a hands-on example to cement the concepts: a glowing rune stone with baked GI. First, create a Plane for the ground and a Cube for the rune stone; position the cube slightly above the plane. Mark both objects as Static in the Inspector so they will be included in lightmapping. Next, create a new material M_RuneStone and assign it to the cube. For the base look, choose a dark gray Albedo, set Metallic to 0.1 and Smoothness to 0.2 to simulate rough stone. Under Emission, check the Emission box, pick a vibrant blue Emission Color and set Intensity to about 5. Assign a black-and-white rune Emission map so only the rune pattern glows. In the Emission section set Global Illumination to Baked. For contrast, add a low-intensity Point Light with a warm orange color and intensity around 0.5. Open Lighting settings, ensure Auto Generate is off, then click Generate Lighting. After baking, inspect the lightmap and scene: the surrounding plane should receive a soft blue tint from the emission combined with the warm orange from the point light. As a practice variation, change the Emission Color to red and re-bake to observe how the indirect light color changes.

As a practice variation, change the Emission Color to red and re-bake to observe how the indirect light color changes.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Glowing Rune Stone
Step-by-step
Follow these steps in Unity to author an emissive rune that contributes to baked GI.
1. Scene setup
Create a Plane and Cube, position cube slightly above plane, and mark both Static in the Inspector.
2. Material
Create M_RuneStone, set Albedo to dark gray, Metallic 0.1, Smoothness 0.2, enable Emission, choose blue color and Intensity 5, assign black-and-white rune texture to Emission map.
3. GI and lighting
Set Emission 'Global Illumination' to Baked, add a Point Light with intensity ~0.5 and warm color for contrast, open Lighting Settings and generate lighting.
Expected result
After baking, nearby static surfaces show a soft blue tint from the rune emission blended with the orange point light.
Variation
Change Emission Color to red and re-bake to see how indirect lighting color shifts in the lightmaps.
Key Takeaway

This practical flow shows how to author emission and include it in baked GI for a convincing, performance-friendly glow.

screens.title: Baking Lighting: Inspect, Tune, and Rebake
screens.narratorSegment: After setting emission and GI modes, baking is where you verify that the glow affects the scene as intended. First, inspect the Lighting window options: check your lightmap resolution, padding, and whether Auto Generate is on. For controlled iteration, uncheck Auto Generate and use manual 'Generate Lighting' so you can make deliberate changes between bakes. Once the bake completes, inspect the lightmaps in the Lighting window and view the scene in the Editor to check color bleeding and intensity. If the emission tint is too faint, increase Emission Intensity or adjust the Emission map's white levels and re-bake. If the glow is too strong and washes out detail, lower intensity or reduce emission area in the texture. Always test with the same exposure and post-processing settings used in-game so bakes match runtime perception. Keep an eye on lightmap memory usage: increasing resolution will increase quality but also build time and memory. A practical experiment is to toggle the Point Light off and on before rebaking to compare emission-only versus emission-plus-point-light results. This helps you decide whether to rely on baked emission or to include a low-cost real light for directional cues.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Bake & Iterate
Bake checklist
Use controlled bakes to tune emission impact and manage cost.
1. Bake control
Turn off Auto Generate if you want manual iteration. Adjust lightmap resolution and padding with care.
2. Tune emission
If tint is weak, increase intensity or tweak the map; if too bright, lower intensity or reduce emissive area.
3. Compare results
Bake with and without the Point Light to evaluate emission-only versus combined lighting approaches.
Memory note
Higher lightmap resolution improves quality but increases memory and bake time; optimize per target platform.
Misconception
A single bake will not automatically match runtime exposure changes; bake with final post-processing settings to match in-game appearance.
Key Takeaway

Bake intentionally: iterate emission and lightmap settings, compare emission-only and mixed lighting, and monitor memory and build time when increasing resolution.

screens.title: Emission-only vs Emission + Point Light
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing emission-only setups to a mixed approach that combines emission with a subtle Point Light helps you choose what to use per scene. Emission-only makes surfaces appear self-lit and is ideal for decorative glows where directional shadows are unimportant. It is cheaper when baked for static scenes because it can be stored in lightmaps. However, emission-only lacks directional cues and does not create sharp shadows. Adding a low-intensity Point Light near the emissive surface provides directional shading and a soft shadow anchor, increasing readability and giving players a better sense of spatial relationships. For example, a neon sign with only emission will glow but the scene may lack clear shadow direction; adding a dim Point Light preserves the sign’s glow while casting a small shadow that clarifies depth. The tradeoff is runtime cost: a single low-cost Point Light is often cheaper than enabling realtime GI for moving emissive objects. A misconception is that a Point Light will always replace emission; instead, use the Point Light for shadows and direction and use emission for local pixel brightness and stylistic glow. Decide based on movement, performance budget, and the visual clarity you need.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Emission vs Emission+Point
Emission-only
Pure emission visually brightens pixels without adding directional shadows; best for decorative effects and baked GI.
Pros
Cheap when baked, strong stylistic glow, useful for screens and neon.
Cons
Lacks directional cues and shadows; can wash out details if intensity is too high.
Emission + Point Light
Combine emission for pixel brightness and a low-intensity Point Light for directional lighting and soft shadows that increase readability.
Pros
Adds spatial cues, small shadows, and depth while preserving emission aesthetics.
Cost
A single low-intensity Point Light is often cheaper than enabling realtime GI for dynamics and provides better directional readability.
Check Your Understanding

If your emissive object must move and tint surroundings, consider if realtime GI is required. Otherwise, bake emission and add a small Point Light for directional clarity.

screens.title: Pitfalls and Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When working with emission and GI, three common mistakes can degrade visuals or performance. First, over-bright emission intensity can wash out texture detail and create unrealistic, blown-out areas; tune intensity and test under final exposure and post-processing. Second, relying on realtime Global Illumination when not needed increases runtime cost and can cause inconsistent frame rates; prefer baked GI for static emitters and use realtime GI only when objects move or change intensity. Third, using excessively large lightmap resolutions for small scene benefits will inflate memory and build times. Optimize by baking at a lower resolution for distant geometry and higher resolution only where proximity requires detail. Another pitfall is forgetting to mark emissive objects as Static — without that, emission won’t be baked into lightmaps. Finally, do not assume emission can replace directional lights; if you need shadows or strong directional cues, add a modest Point or Spot light. A useful rule is to test on target hardware early: bake a scene with your emissive elements and measure build time and memory, then adjust resolution and GI choices to meet performance targets.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Pitfalls & Performance
Common mistakes
Watch for these frequent errors when using emission and GI.
Over-bright emission
High intensity can hide surface detail and break perceived material properties; test with final exposure settings.
Unnecessary realtime GI
Use realtime GI only when objects move or emission changes at runtime; otherwise prefer baked GI for performance.
Oversized lightmaps
Large resolutions increase build times and memory; tune resolution per-object and per-platform.
Static flag omission
Forgetting to mark objects static prevents emission from being included in baked lightmaps.
Key Takeaway

Tune emission and bake settings thoughtfully, prefer baked GI for fixed glow, and profile on target hardware to avoid runtime surprises.

screens.title: Key Concepts: Light Types & Emission
screens.narratorSegment: Remember these concise definitions as you author materials and lights. Directional Light simulates a distant, sun-like source with parallel rays and consistent shadows across the scene. Point Light emits from a single point in all directions with radial falloff, useful for bulbs and local light sources. Spot Light emits in a cone for focused, directional illumination. Keep these differences in mind when placing lights; each will change how materials read and how highlights form. These three light types form the basic vocabulary you'll use for composition and for deciding whether emission or actual lights are needed to produce the desired visual cues. In practical terms, core definitions to keep handy while authoring scenes.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on a single, high-value skill: making materials behave believably under different lights and using emission to add atmosphere. You will learn how Directional, Point, and Spot lights create distinct highlights and shadows on PBR materials, why Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness change those responses, and how an Emission map makes parts of a surface appear to glow. We’ll also cover the crucial difference between visible emission and emission that contributes to indirect lighting, and the practical steps to mark an object static and include its emission in baked Global Illumination. This matters because believable lighting is what sells mood and materiality in game environments. A glowing rune can be purely decorative, or it can actually tint nearby surfaces when baked correctly — the difference affects realism and performance. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to set up a glowing rune stone, choose the right GI mode, and avoid common pitfalls like over-bright emission or unnecessary real-time GI costs. Think of this as the toolset you use when light needs to both look right and behave affordably.

These objectives break the chapter into practical skills. First, you will explain how different light types — Directional, Point, and Spot — interact with PBR material properties so you can predict highlights and shadows. Knowing this helps you place lights to sell material realism. Second, you will understand Emission maps: how a black-and-white texture controls which pixels glow, and how to set color and intensity so glow reads correctly in scenes. Third, you will differentiate between real-time and baked lighting, recognizing when to use each approach for dynamic elements versus static environment pieces. Finally, you will configure a material to contribute to Global Illumination by setting the material’s Emission GI mode and marking objects static before baking. Each objective emphasizes a concrete inspector step or a decision rule you can apply in Unity. Together these skills let you create visually convincing glowing elements while staying mindful of performance and the limits of emission versus actual light sources.

These secondary objectives focus on practical behavior and common mistakes. First, you will learn to identify when emission is only visual versus when it needs to contribute to indirect lighting; that choice drives whether you set emission to Baked or Realtime in the material. Second, you will practice the bake workflow: marking objects static, disabling automatic generation, and manually generating lighting so emission is captured in the lightmap. Third, you will spot performance traps like over-reliance on real-time GI or very high-resolution lightmaps and learn alternatives. Finally, you will be able to compare an emission-only approach with a mixed approach that uses a low-intensity point light for directional cues. Together these competencies help you find a balance between visual fidelity and runtime cost, and give you an actionable checklist to apply in scene setup and optimization.

Start by identifying what each Unity light type is meant to simulate and why that matters for materials. Directional lights act like the sun: they send parallel rays across the scene and create consistent full-scene illumination and long, crisp shadows. Use them where you need a dominant, uniform light source. Point lights emit from a single point in all directions and are ideal for bulbs or embers; they produce radial falloff so highlights are localized and bright near the source but dim quickly with distance. Spot lights are a constrained point light that emits inside a cone, useful for flashlights or stage lights that need both directionality and a falloff profile. Concretely, on a PBR sphere a highly metallic, smooth surface will show a hard, small highlight from a point light and a softer elongated highlight from a directional source. A rough surface diffuses those highlights into broad soft patches. A common misconception is to treat all lights as interchangeable: the visual cues and shadow behavior are different and affect perceived material type. To practice, place a neutral PBR sphere, toggle lights on and off, and observe how the same material reads metallic under one light and matte under another. Which light makes the material read as polished or worn? That observation will guide your placement decisions in a scene and help you balance realism with performance.

To predict how a material will look under lighting, you need a clear definition of the core PBR channels. Albedo defines the base color that diffusely reflects light. It controls the hue and visible surface pigmentation that remains under diffuse illumination. Metallic is a boolean-like range that decides whether reflections carry the surface tint (metallic) or remain neutral (dielectric). A metallic surface reflects environment colors strongly and darkens its diffuse contribution, while a non-metal retains its albedo as the diffuse result. Smoothness controls microfacet distribution: higher smoothness yields narrow, high-intensity specular highlights that mirror the light source, while low smoothness scatters reflection energy into broad, soft highlights. Concretely, a bright point light on a smooth metal creates a crisp pinprick highlight; on a rough non-metal it becomes a soft, spread highlight. A common mistake is to push smoothness and metallic values to extremes without considering environment reflections and exposure controls — this can yield blown-out highlights or a plastic look. Practice adjusting each channel on the same geometry while keeping lighting constant: you’ll see how simple numeric changes dramatically alter material read and perceived realism.

An Emission map is a texture that tells the shader which parts of a surface should appear lit regardless of scene lighting. White areas in the emission texture produce full emission, black areas have none, and gray values yield partial emission. You can pair that map with an Emission Color and an Intensity multiplier to control hue and perceived brightness. Artistically, emission is perfect for screens, neon, glowing veins, or magical runes. Technically, emission overrides the normal lighting calculation for those pixels and makes them render as if they are bright. A key practical note: by default emission only affects the object's own shading; it makes pixels look bright but does not necessarily light other objects. To make emission contribute to scene lighting you must enable its Global Illumination contribution and select a baked or realtime mode depending on your needs. A common error is using very high emission intensity without adjusting exposure and post-processing, which can blow out details and hide texture contrast. When authoring emission maps, keep the pattern clear, preview the result in different exposure settings, and test both with and without additional explicit light sources for directional cues.

A recurring source of confusion is the difference between emission as a visual effect and emission as a contributor to scene lighting. By default, enabling Emission on a material makes pixels render as if they are bright, but that brightness is local to the object’s shader; it affects how the object looks to the camera, not necessarily how it lights neighboring geometry. To make emission influence the rest of the scene, you must enable Global Illumination on the material and pick either Baked or Realtime in the Emission GI dropdown. Baked GI records emission into lightmaps for static geometry, allowing glowing objects to tint nearby surfaces affordably. Realtime GI, if available and enabled, allows dynamic objects to contribute to indirect lighting but at a higher runtime cost. An example: a glowing rune on a static stone with Emission GI set to Baked will create a subtle colored bleed onto surrounding walls after baking. A common mistake is assuming emission replaces actual lights; emission adds ambient tint but does not cast precise shadows or directional illumination. When you need directional cues and crisp shadows, combine emission with a low-intensity Point or Spot light for the right mix of atmosphere and readable lighting.

Global Illumination simulates how light bounces and contributes to the indirect illumination in a scene. There are two practical approaches you will use in Unity: baked lighting and realtime lighting. Baked lighting precomputes indirect lighting into lightmaps for static geometry; this is extremely efficient at runtime and produces stable, high-quality indirect lighting for environments that do not change. Realtime lighting updates every frame and allows dynamic objects and lights to affect indirect illumination, but it costs more C P U or G P U time and can be harder to optimize. For emission, baked GI is the most common approach: set Emission GI to Baked, mark the glowing object as static, and generate lighting so the emission is stored into the lightmap and tints neighboring surfaces. Realtime GI should be reserved for cases where glowing elements move or change intensity at runtime and your target platform can afford the cost. A common confusion is thinking baked lightmaps are low-quality; when tuned with proper resolution and bake settings, they provide natural-looking indirect color bleeding without the runtime expense. Choose the method that balances visual fidelity and platform performance for your project.

Begin by selecting your material in the Project window. In the material Inspector find the Emission section, check the Emission checkbox, and assign your Emission map and color. Next, select the object using that material in the Hierarchy and set its 'Static' checkbox in the top-right of the Inspector so Unity considers it for lightmapping. A common oversight is forgetting to mark the object static or leaving Emission GI on 'None'; either omission will stop indirect illumination from being saved. Always re-bake after making changes to emission color or intensity, because lightmaps are generated from the current emission settings at bake time.
